leaves.title: I am
leaves.explanation: Use 'am' with the subject 'I' in the present tense. Example: I am a teacher.

leaves.title: I am not
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after 'am' to make a negative statement with 'I'. Example: I am not tired.

leaves.title: Am I ...?
leaves.explanation: Put 'Am' before 'I' to ask a yes/no question. Example: Am I late?

leaves.title: Am I not ...?
leaves.explanation: Put 'Am' before 'I' and add 'not' to ask a negative question. Example: Am I not invited?

leaves.title: You are
leaves.explanation: Use 'are' with the subject 'you' in the present tense. Example: You are my friend.

leaves.title: You are not
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after 'are' to make a negative statement with 'you'. Example: You are not ready.

leaves.title: Are you ...?
leaves.explanation: Put 'Are' before 'you' to ask a yes/no question. Example: Are you hungry?

leaves.title: Aren't you ...?
leaves.explanation: Use the contraction 'Aren't' before 'you' to ask a negative question. Example: Aren't you coming?

leaves.title: he/she is
leaves.explanation: Use 'is' with 'he' or 'she' in the present tense. Example: She is a doctor.

leaves.title: he/she is not
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after 'is' to make a negative statement with 'he/she'. Example: He is not home.

leaves.title: Is he/she ...?
leaves.explanation: Put 'Is' before 'he/she' to ask a yes/no question. Example: Is she okay?

leaves.title: Isn't he/she ...?
leaves.explanation: Use the contraction 'Isn't' before 'he/she' to ask a negative question. Example: Isn't he your brother?

leaves.title: we are
leaves.explanation: Use 'are' with the subject 'we' in the present tense. Example: We are students.

leaves.title: we are not
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after 'are' to make a negative statement with 'we'. Example: We are not late.

leaves.title: Are we ...?
leaves.explanation: Put 'Are' before 'we' to ask a yes/no question. Example: Are we early?

leaves.title: Aren't we ...?
leaves.explanation: Use the contraction 'Aren't' before 'we' to ask a negative question. Example: Aren't we invited?

leaves.title: they are
leaves.explanation: Use 'are' with the subject 'they' in the present tense. Example: They are neighbours.

leaves.title: they are not
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after 'are' to make a negative statement with 'they'. Example: They are not here.

leaves.title: Are they ...?
leaves.explanation: Put 'Are' before 'they' to ask a yes/no question. Example: Are they ready?

leaves.title: Aren't they ...?
leaves.explanation: Use the contraction 'Aren't' before 'they' to ask a negative question. Example: Aren't they coming too?

leaves.title: my/our/your/her/their (except for 'his' and 'its')
leaves.explanation: Use 'my/our/your/her/their' before a noun to show who it belongs to. Example: This is my book.

leaves.title: me/us/him/her/them (except for 'you' and 'it')
leaves.explanation: Use 'me/us/him/her/them' as the object of a verb or preposition. Example: Give it to me.

leaves.title: This/That is
leaves.explanation: Use 'This/That is' to point out one nearby or distant thing. Example: This is my bag.

leaves.title: This/That is not
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after 'is' to make a negative statement with 'This/That'. Example: That is not mine.

leaves.title: Is this/that ...?
leaves.explanation: Put 'Is' before 'this/that' to ask a yes/no question. Example: Is this yours?

leaves.title: Isn't this/that ...?
leaves.explanation: Use the contraction 'Isn't' before 'this/that' to ask a negative question. Example: Isn't that expensive?

leaves.title: These/Those are
leaves.explanation: Use 'These/Those are' to point out several nearby or distant things. Example: These are my keys.

leaves.title: These/Those are not
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after 'are' to make a negative statement with 'These/Those'. Example: Those are not mine.

leaves.title: Are these/those ...?
leaves.explanation: Put 'Are' before 'these/those' to ask a yes/no question. Example: Are these fresh?

leaves.title: Aren't these/those ...?
leaves.explanation: Use the contraction 'Aren't' before 'these/those' to ask a negative question. Example: Aren't those yours?

leaves.title: It is
leaves.explanation: Use 'It is' to describe or identify a thing, time, or situation. Example: It is raining.

leaves.title: It is not
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after 'is' to make a negative statement with 'It'. Example: It is not far.

leaves.title: Is it ...?
leaves.explanation: Put 'Is' before 'it' to ask a yes/no question. Example: Is it cold outside?

leaves.title: Isn't it ...?
leaves.explanation: Use the contraction 'Isn't' before 'it' to ask a negative question. Example: Isn't it beautiful?

leaves.title: This/That N
leaves.explanation: Use 'This/That' directly before a singular noun to point it out. Example: This car is new.

leaves.title: These/Those N
leaves.explanation: Use 'These/Those' directly before a plural noun to point them out. Example: Those shoes are nice.

leaves.title: INDEFINITE ARTICLES
leaves.explanation: Use 'a' or 'an' before a singular countable noun when it is not specific. Example: I saw a cat.

leaves.title: DEFINITE ARTICLES
leaves.explanation: Use 'the' before a noun when both speaker and listener know which one is meant. Example: Close the door.

leaves.title: DETERMINERS: some/any
leaves.explanation: Use 'some' in positive sentences and 'any' in questions/negatives for an unspecified quantity. Example: I need some water. Do you have any milk?

leaves.title: DETERMINER: no
leaves.explanation: Use 'no' directly before a noun to mean 'not any'. Example: There is no milk left.

leaves.title: DETERMINER: another
leaves.explanation: Use 'another' to mean 'one more' or 'a different one'. Example: Can I have another coffee?

leaves.title: much UNCOUNTABLE NOUN
leaves.explanation: Use 'much' before an uncountable noun to talk about a large quantity. Example: There isn't much time.

leaves.title: little UNCOUNTABLE NOUN
leaves.explanation: Use 'little' before an uncountable noun to mean a small amount. Example: We have little information.

leaves.title: few PLURAL NOUN
leaves.explanation: Use 'few' before a plural noun to mean not many. Example: Few people know the answer.

leaves.title: PREPOSITIONS
leaves.explanation: Prepositions link a noun/pronoun to another word to show place, time, or direction. Example: The book is on the table.

leaves.title: POSSESSIVE PRONOUNS (except for 'his' and 'its')
leaves.explanation: Use possessive pronouns (mine, ours, yours, hers, theirs) to replace 'noun + 's'. Example: This pen is mine.

leaves.title: REFLEXIVE PRONOUNS
leaves.explanation: Use reflexive pronouns (myself, yourself, etc.) when the subject and object of a verb are the same person. Example: She hurt herself.

leaves.title: INDEFINITE PRONOUNS
leaves.explanation: Indefinite pronouns (someone, anything, everybody, etc.) refer to people or things without naming them. Example: Someone called you.

leaves.title: INDEFINITE PRONOUN/PROP-WORDS: ones (except for 'one')
leaves.explanation: Use 'ones' to replace a plural noun already mentioned. Example: I like the red ones.

leaves.title: INDEFINITE PRONOUN: none
leaves.explanation: Use 'none' to mean 'not one' or 'not any' of a group. Example: None of them arrived.

leaves.title: RECIPROCAL PRONOUN: each other
leaves.explanation: Use 'each other' when two people do the same thing to one another. Example: They helped each other.

leaves.title: RECIPROCAL PRONOUN: one another
leaves.explanation: Use 'one another' when more than two people do the same thing to each other. Example: The team supported one another.

leaves.title: PRONOUN: others (excluding 'the
leaves.explanation: Use 'others' to mean additional people or things of the same kind, excluding those already mentioned. Example: Some left early; others stayed.

leaves.title: PRONOUNS: the other/others
leaves.explanation: Use 'the other/others' to refer to the remaining specific person(s) or thing(s) in a group. Example: One shoe is here; where's the other?

leaves.title: -thing ADJ
leaves.explanation: Add '-thing' words like 'something/nothing' before an adjective to describe them. Example: I want something new.

leaves.title: ADVERBS OF FREQUENCY: always/usually/often/frequently/occasionally/sometimes/rarely
leaves.explanation: Adverbs of frequency (always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely) show how often something happens. Example: I usually walk to work.

leaves.title: ADVERBS: INTENSIFIERS: extremely/greatly/really/so/terribly/too/unbelievably/very
leaves.explanation: Intensifying adverbs (very, really, extremely, so, too) strengthen the meaning of an adjective or adverb. Example: It's extremely hot today.

leaves.title: ADVERBS OF ATTITUDES: apparently/clearly/fortunately/frankly/unfortunately
leaves.explanation: Attitude adverbs (apparently, clearly, fortunately, unfortunately) show the speaker's opinion about a whole sentence. Example: Unfortunately, the shop was closed.

leaves.title: ADVERBS OF NEGATION: never
leaves.explanation: Use 'never' to mean 'at no time' — it makes a sentence negative without using 'not'. Example: I never eat meat.

leaves.title: ADVERBS OF QUASI-NEGATION: hardly/little/scarcely/seldom
leaves.explanation: Adverbs like 'hardly, scarcely, seldom' express near-negative meaning. Example: I can hardly hear you.

leaves.title: COMPARISON OF EQUALITY: as ... as
leaves.explanation: Use 'as ... as' to say two things are equal in some way. Example: She is as tall as her brother.

leaves.title: COMPARISON OF EQUALITY: not as/so ... as
leaves.grammarPoint: COMPARISON OF EQUALITY: not as/so ... as
leaves.explanation: Use 'not as/so ... as' to say one thing is less than another. Example: This book is not as good as the last one.

leaves.title: COMPARATIVE OF SUPERIORITY: -er
leaves.explanation: Add '-er' to short adjectives/adverbs to compare two things. Example: This bag is bigger than that one.

leaves.title: COMPARATIVE OF SUPERIORITY: more+ADJ/ADV
leaves.explanation: Use 'more' before longer adjectives/adverbs to compare two things. Example: This film is more interesting than the last.

leaves.title: SUPERLATIVE OF SUPERIORITY: -est
leaves.explanation: Add '-est' to short adjectives/adverbs to show the highest degree among three or more. Example: She is the tallest in her class.

leaves.title: SUPERLATIVE OF SUPERIORITY: most+ADJ/ADV
leaves.explanation: Use 'most' before longer adjectives/adverbs to show the highest degree. Example: It's the most beautiful place I've seen.

leaves.title: COMPARATIVE/SUPERLATIVE OF INFERIORITY
leaves.explanation: Irregular comparatives/superlatives of inferiority use 'less' and 'least'. Example: This is less useful than that one.

leaves.title: ADJ/ADV enough (except for 'not enough')
leaves.explanation: Use 'enough' after an adjective/adverb to mean 'as much as needed'. Example: He is old enough to drive.

leaves.title: too ADJ/ADV to+INFINITIVE
leaves.explanation: Use 'too + adjective/adverb + to + infinitive' to show something is more than needed, preventing an action. Example: It's too hot to go outside.

leaves.title: so ADJ/ADV (that) CLAUSE
leaves.explanation: Use 'so + adjective/adverb + that' to show a result. Example: She was so tired that she fell asleep.

leaves.title: such (a/an) ADJ NOUN
leaves.explanation: Use 'such (a/an) + adjective + noun' to show a result or emphasis. Example: It was such a good film.

leaves.title: so ADJ a/an NOUN
leaves.explanation: Use 'so + adjective + a/an + noun' as an alternative word order to 'such a'. Example: It was so good a film.

leaves.title: too ADJ a/an NOUN
leaves.explanation: Use 'too + adjective + a/an + noun' to show excess before a singular noun. Example: It's too big a decision.

leaves.title: COMPARATIVE and COMPARATIVE (the same adjective)
leaves.explanation: Repeat a comparative form joined by 'and' to show continuous change. Example: It's getting colder and colder.

leaves.title: the COMPARATIVE (...), the COMPARATIVE
leaves.explanation: Use 'the + comparative ..., the + comparative ...' to link two changes together. Example: The more you practice, the better you get.

leaves.title: INTENSIFIED COMPARATIVES: a lot/by far/even/far/much/still
leaves.explanation: Use intensifiers like 'a lot, much, far, even, still' before a comparative to strengthen it. Example: This is much better.

leaves.title: INTENSIFIED SUPERLATIVES: by far/far/far and away/much
leaves.grammarPoint: INTENSIFIED SUPERLATIVES: by far/far/far and away/much
leaves.explanation: Use intensifiers like 'by far, far and away' before a superlative to strengthen it. Example: She is by far the best.

leaves.title: do/does DO
leaves.explanation: Use 'do/does' as an auxiliary verb for present simple questions and negatives. Example: Do you like tea? He doesn't like coffee.

leaves.title: did DO
leaves.explanation: Use 'did' as the auxiliary verb for past simple questions and negatives. Example: Did you see that? I didn't go.

leaves.title: PHRASAL VERBS (V+PARTICLE)
leaves.explanation: Phrasal verbs made of verb + particle (no object between them). Example: The plane took off.

leaves.title: PHRASAL VERBS (V+NP+PARTICLE)
leaves.explanation: Phrasal verbs made of verb + noun/pronoun + particle. Example: She picked the book up.

leaves.title: PHRASAL VERBS (V+PARTICLE+PREP+NP)
leaves.explanation: Phrasal verbs made of verb + particle + preposition + noun. Example: I look forward to seeing you.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (BE) — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'am/is/are' to describe a current state or identity. Example: I am happy.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (BE) — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after am/is/are to make a negative statement about a current state. Example: She is not busy.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (BE) — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert the verb 'be' and the subject to ask a question about a current state. Example: Are you ready?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (BE) — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a contracted negative form ('isn't/aren't') before the subject to ask a negative question. Example: Isn't he tired?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (lexical verbs) — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use the base verb (or -s for he/she/it) to talk about habits, facts, and routines. Example: I play tennis every week.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (lexical verbs) — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'don't/doesn't + base verb' to make a present simple statement negative. Example: They don't work on Sundays.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (lexicalverbs)
leaves.explanation: Use 'Do/Does + subject + base verb' to ask a present simple question. Example: Does she like coffee?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (lexical verbs) — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Don't/Doesn't + subject + base verb' to ask a negative present simple question. Example: Don't you like pizza?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (lexical verbs; third person & singular) — AFF. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (lexical verbs; third person & singular) — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add '-s' or '-es' to the base verb for he/she/it in the present simple. Example: He plays football.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (lexical verbs; third person & singular) — NEG. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (lexical verbs; third person & singular) — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'doesn't + base verb' for a negative present simple sentence with he/she/it. Example: She doesn't drink coffee.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (lexical verbs; third person & singular) — AFF. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (lexical verbs; third person & singular) — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Does + he/she/it + base verb' to ask a present simple question about a third person. Example: Does it work?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (lexical verbs; third person & singular) — NEG. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (lexical verbs; third person & singular) — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Doesn't + he/she/it + base verb' to ask a negative present simple question about a third person. Example: Doesn't he know?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT PROGRESSIVE — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'am/is/are + verb-ing' to talk about an action happening now. Example: I am reading a book.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT PROGRESSIVE — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after am/is/are + verb-ing to make it negative. Example: She is not listening.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT PROGRESSIVE — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert 'be' and the subject before verb-ing to ask a question about now. Example: Are you working?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT PROGRESSIVE — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a contracted negative 'be' form before the subject and verb-ing. Example: Isn't he sleeping?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT PERFECT — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'have/has + past participle' to connect the past to the present. Example: I have finished my homework.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT PERFECT — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'haven't/hasn't + past participle' to make a present perfect statement negative. Example: She hasn't arrived yet.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT PERFECT — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Have/Has + subject + past participle' to ask a present perfect question. Example: Have you seen this film?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT PERFECT — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Haven't/Hasn't + subject + past participle' to ask a negative present perfect question. Example: Haven't they left yet?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — AFF. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'have/has been + verb-ing' to emphasise the duration of an ongoing action up to now. Example: I have been studying for two hours.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — NEG. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after have/has been to make it negative. Example: She hasn't been feeling well.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — AFF. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Have/Has + subject + been + verb-ing' to ask about an ongoing action's duration. Example: Have you been waiting long?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — NEG. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask about an ongoing action's duration. Example: Haven't you been sleeping well?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST (BE) — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'was/were' to describe a past state. Example: I was tired yesterday.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST (BE) — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after was/were to make a past state negative. Example: They were not at home.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST (BE) — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert 'was/were' and the subject to ask a question about a past state. Example: Were you at the party?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST (BE) — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a contracted negative past 'be' form before the subject. Example: Wasn't she there?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (lexical verbs) — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use the past simple (often -ed) for a completed action at a specific past time. Example: I visited Paris last year.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (lexical verbs) — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'didn't + base verb' to make a past simple statement negative. Example: We didn't go to school.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (lexical verbs) — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Did + subject + base verb' to ask a past simple question. Example: Did you call her?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (lexical verbs) — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Didn't + subject + base verb' to ask a negative past simple question. Example: Didn't you finish it?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST PROGRESSIVE — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'was/were + verb-ing' for an action in progress at a past moment. Example: I was cooking when you called.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST PROGRESSIVE — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after was/were + verb-ing to make it negative. Example: They weren't listening.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST PROGRESSIVE — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert 'was/were' and the subject before verb-ing to ask a question. Example: Were you sleeping?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST PROGRESSIVE — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a contracted negative 'be' form before the subject and verb-ing. Example: Wasn't he watching TV?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST PERFECT — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'had + past participle' for an action completed before another past action. Example: I had left before she arrived.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST PERFECT — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after 'had' to make a past perfect statement negative. Example: We hadn't eaten yet.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST PERFECT — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Had + subject + past participle' to ask a past perfect question. Example: Had you met her before?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST PERFECT — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Hadn't + subject + past participle' to ask a negative past perfect question. Example: Hadn't they finished?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — AFF. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'had been + verb-ing' for an action in progress before another past action. Example: I had been waiting for an hour when she arrived.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — NEG. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after 'had been' to make it negative. Example: They hadn't been listening.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — AFF. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Had + subject + been + verb-ing' to ask about an ongoing past action before another. Example: Had you been waiting long?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — NEG. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask about an ongoing past action before another. Example: Hadn't they been working there?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'will + base verb' to talk about future predictions or decisions made now. Example: I will call you tomorrow.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'won't + base verb' to make a future statement negative. Example: She won't come.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Will + subject + base verb' to ask a future question. Example: Will you help me?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Won't + subject + base verb' to ask a negative future question. Example: Won't you join us?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'going to + base verb' for a planned future intention. Example: We are going to travel next year.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to make a 'going to' future statement negative. Example: I'm not going to wait.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE PROGRESSIVE — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'will be + verb-ing' to ask about an action in progress at a future time. Example: Will you be working late?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE PROGRESSIVE — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask about a future action in progress. Example: Won't you be joining us?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE PERFECT — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'will have + past participle' for an action completed before a future point. Example: I will have finished by Friday.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE PERFECT — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after 'will have' to make it negative. Example: She won't have arrived yet.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE PERFECT — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Will + subject + have + past participle' to ask about a future completed action. Example: Will you have finished?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE PERFECT — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask about a future completed action. Example: Won't they have left?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — AFF. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'will have been + verb-ing' to emphasise duration of an action up to a future point. Example: By June, I will have been working here for ten years.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — NEG. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after 'will have been' to make it negative. Example: They won't have been waiting long.

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — AFF. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Will + subject + have been + verb-ing' to ask about a future action's duration. Example: Will you have been studying long?

leaves.title: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — NEG. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE PERFECT PROGRESSIVE — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask about a future action's duration. Example: Won't she have been working there long?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PRESENT — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'am/is/are + past participle' to focus on the receiver of a present action. Example: The room is cleaned every day.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PRESENT — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to make a present passive statement negative. Example: The letters are not delivered on Sundays.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PRESENT — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert 'be' and the subject to ask a present passive question. Example: Is the work finished?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PRESENT — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a present passive question. Example: Isn't it done yet?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PRESENT PROGRESSIVE — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'am/is/are being + past participle' for a passive action happening now. Example: The car is being repaired.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PRESENT PROGRESSIVE — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to make a present progressive passive statement negative. Example: The road isn't being fixed today.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PRESENT PROGRESSIVE — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert 'be' and the subject before 'being' to ask a question. Example: Is the house being painted?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PRESENT PROGRESSIVE — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a present progressive passive question. Example: Isn't it being cleaned?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PRESENT PERFECT — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'have/has been + past participle' for a passive action linking past to present. Example: The email has been sent.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PRESENT PERFECT — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after have/has to make a present perfect passive statement negative. Example: The report hasn't been finished.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PRESENT PERFECT — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Have/Has + subject + been + past participle' to ask a present perfect passive question. Example: Has the package been delivered?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PRESENT PERFECT — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a present perfect passive question. Example: Hasn't it been fixed yet?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PAST — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'was/were + past participle' to focus on the receiver of a past action. Example: The window was broken.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PAST — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to make a past passive statement negative. Example: The bill wasn't paid.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PAST — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert 'was/were' and the subject to ask a past passive question. Example: Was the house built recently?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PAST — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a past passive question. Example: Wasn't it repaired last week?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PAST PROGRESSIVE — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'was/were being + past participle' for a passive action in progress at a past moment. Example: The bridge was being built when I visited.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PAST PROGRESSIVE — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to make a past progressive passive statement negative. Example: The car wasn't being used.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PAST PROGRESSIVE — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert 'was/were' and the subject before 'being' to ask a question. Example: Was the meeting being recorded?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PAST PROGRESSIVE — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a past progressive passive question. Example: Wasn't it being repaired?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PAST PERFECT — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'had been + past participle' for a passive action completed before another past action. Example: The house had been sold before we arrived.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PAST PERFECT — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after 'had' to make a past perfect passive statement negative. Example: The letter hadn't been sent.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PAST PERFECT — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Had + subject + been + past participle' to ask a past perfect passive question. Example: Had the work been finished?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: PAST PERFECT — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a past perfect passive question. Example: Hadn't it been done already?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: FUTURE — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'will be + past participle' for a passive action expected in the future. Example: The results will be announced tomorrow.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: FUTURE — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after 'will' to make a future passive statement negative. Example: The event won't be cancelled.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: FUTURE — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Will + subject + be + past participle' to ask a future passive question. Example: Will the report be finished?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: FUTURE — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a future passive question. Example: Won't it be fixed by then?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: FUTURE PROGRESSIVE — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'will be being + past participle' for a passive action in progress at a future point. Example: The house will be being renovated next month.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: FUTURE PROGRESSIVE — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to make a future progressive passive statement negative. Example: It won't be being used then.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: FUTURE PROGRESSIVE — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Will + subject + be being + past participle' to ask a future progressive passive question. Example: Will it be being repaired then?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: FUTURE PROGRESSIVE — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a future progressive passive question. Example: Won't it be being cleaned?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: FUTURE PERFECT — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'will have been + past participle' for a passive action completed before a future point. Example: The building will have been finished by June.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: FUTURE PERFECT — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after 'will have' to make it negative. Example: It won't have been repaired by then.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: FUTURE PERFECT — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Will + subject + have been + past participle' to ask a future perfect passive question. Example: Will it have been completed?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: FUTURE PERFECT — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a future perfect passive question. Example: Won't it have been fixed?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: AUX — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use a modal + 'be + past participle' to form a passive with modal meaning. Example: This must be done today.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: AUX — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after the modal to make a modal passive statement negative. Example: This mustn't be forgotten.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: AUX — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert the modal and subject to ask a modal passive question. Example: Should this be done now?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: AUX — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a modal passive question. Example: Shouldn't this be checked?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: AUX+PROGRESSIVE — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use a modal + 'be being + past participle' for a modal passive action in progress. Example: It might be being fixed right now.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: AUX+PROGRESSIVE — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to make a modal progressive passive statement negative. Example: It can't be being used.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: AUX+PROGRESSIVE — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert the modal and subject before 'being' to ask a question. Example: Could it be being repaired?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: AUX+PROGRESSIVE — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a modal progressive passive question. Example: Shouldn't it be being cleaned?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: AUX+PERFECT — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use a modal + 'have been + past participle' for a modal passive about a completed action. Example: It should have been finished by now.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: AUX+PERFECT — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to make a modal perfect passive statement negative. Example: It shouldn't have been left there.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: AUX+PERFECT — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert the modal and subject before 'have been' to ask a question. Example: Could it have been fixed?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: AUX+PERFECT — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a modal perfect passive question. Example: Shouldn't it have been done?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: INDIRECT OBJECTS OF GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL AS SUBJECTS — AFF. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: PASSIVE: INDIRECT OBJECTS OF GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL AS SUBJECTS — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: When the indirect object becomes the subject of a passive sentence with verbs like give/send/show. Example: I was given a present.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: INDIRECT OBJECTS OF GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL AS SUBJECTS — NEG. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: PASSIVE: INDIRECT OBJECTS OF GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL AS SUBJECTS — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to make this passive form negative. Example: She wasn't sent the invitation.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: INDIRECT OBJECTS OF GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL AS SUBJECTS — AFF. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: PASSIVE: INDIRECT OBJECTS OF GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL AS SUBJECTS — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert the verb and subject to ask a question in this passive form. Example: Was he shown the report?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: INDIRECT OBJECTS OF GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL AS SUBJECTS — NEG. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: PASSIVE: INDIRECT OBJECTS OF GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL AS SUBJECTS — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a question in this passive form. Example: Wasn't she told the news?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: DIRECT OBJECTS OF GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL AS SUBJECTS — AFF. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: PASSIVE: DIRECT OBJECTS OF GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL AS SUBJECTS — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: When the direct object becomes the subject of a passive sentence with verbs like give/send/show. Example: A present was given to me.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: DIRECT OBJECTS OF GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL AS SUBJECTS — NEG. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: PASSIVE: DIRECT OBJECTS OF GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL AS SUBJECTS — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to make this passive form negative. Example: The letter wasn't sent to him.

leaves.title: PASSIVE: DIRECT OBJECTS OF GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL AS SUBJECTS — AFF. INT
leaves.grammarPoint: PASSIVE: DIRECT OBJECTS OF GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL AS SUBJECTS — AFF. INT
leaves.explanation: Invert the verb and subject to ask a question in this passive form. Example: Was the news told to her?

leaves.title: PASSIVE: DIRECT OBJECTS OF GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL AS SUBJECTS — NEG. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: PASSIVE: DIRECT OBJECTS OF GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL AS SUBJECTS — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a question in this passive form. Example: Wasn't the gift shown to them?

leaves.title: GET+PAST PARTICIPLE
leaves.explanation: Use 'get + past participle' as an informal alternative to 'be + past participle' in the passive. Example: My phone got stolen.

leaves.title: TO-INFINITIVE: to DO (not preceded by 'not')
leaves.explanation: Use 'to + base verb' as the basic form of the to-infinitive. Example: I want to leave.

leaves.title: TO-INFINITIVE: not to DO
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' before 'to' to make a to-infinitive negative. Example: I decided not to go.

leaves.title: TO-INFINITIVE: to have DONE
leaves.explanation: Use 'to have + past participle' for a to-infinitive referring to an earlier time. Example: She seems to have left already.

leaves.title: TO-INFINITIVE: to be DONE
leaves.explanation: Use 'to be + past participle' for a passive to-infinitive. Example: The task needs to be finished.

leaves.title: TO-INFINITIVE: to have been DONE
leaves.explanation: Use 'to have been + past participle' for a passive to-infinitive referring to an earlier time. Example: It appears to have been repaired.

leaves.title: TO-INFINITIVE: WITH NOTIONAL SUBJECT
leaves.explanation: Use 'for + noun/pronoun + to-infinitive' to give the to-infinitive its own subject. Example: It's important for you to arrive early.

leaves.title: -thing to DO
leaves.explanation: Use '-thing + to + base verb' to describe a purpose for something. Example: I need something to eat.

leaves.title: in order to DO
leaves.explanation: Use 'in order to + base verb' to state a purpose formally. Example: She left early in order to catch the train.

leaves.title: in order not to DO
leaves.explanation: Use 'in order not to + base verb' to state a negative purpose formally. Example: He whispered in order not to wake the baby.

leaves.title: so as to DO
leaves.explanation: Use 'so as to + base verb' as an alternative way to state a purpose. Example: I left early so as to avoid traffic.

leaves.title: so as not to DO
leaves.explanation: Use 'so as not to + base verb' to state a negative purpose. Example: Speak quietly so as not to disturb anyone.

leaves.title: BE to DO
leaves.explanation: Use 'be to + base verb' to describe an official arrangement or instruction. Example: The minister is to visit next week.

leaves.title: BE not to DO
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to make 'be to' negative. Example: Staff are not to use this door.

leaves.title: BE about to DO
leaves.explanation: Use 'be about to + base verb' for an action about to happen very soon. Example: The film is about to start.

leaves.title: BE not about to DO
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to make 'be about to' negative. Example: We are not about to give up.

leaves.title: VERB to DO
leaves.explanation: Use 'verb + to-infinitive' when a verb is followed directly by a to-infinitive. Example: I want to help.

leaves.title: VERB not to DO
leaves.explanation: Use 'verb + not + to-infinitive' to negate the action expressed by the to-infinitive. Example: I decided not to help.

leaves.title: VERB OBJECT to DO
leaves.explanation: Use 'verb + object + to-infinitive' when a verb takes an object before the to-infinitive. Example: I asked her to help.

leaves.title: VERB OBJECT not to DO
leaves.explanation: Use 'verb + object + not + to-infinitive' to negate the object's action. Example: I asked her not to leave.

leaves.title: V-ING (not preceded by 'not')
leaves.explanation: Use the '-ing' form of a verb as a noun-like form (gerund). Example: Swimming is good exercise.

leaves.title: not+V-ING
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' before the '-ing' form to negate a gerund. Example: Not smoking is a good decision.

leaves.title: having+PAST PARTICIPLE
leaves.explanation: Use 'having + past participle' as a perfect participle to show one action completed before another. Example: Having finished dinner, we went for a walk.

leaves.title: being+PAST PARTICIPLE
leaves.explanation: Use 'being + past participle' as a passive present participle. Example: Being asked to speak, she felt nervous.

leaves.title: having been+PAST PARTICIPLE
leaves.explanation: Use 'having been + past participle' as a passive perfect participle. Example: Having been warned, he was careful.

leaves.title: PREP+V-ING
leaves.explanation: Use a preposition followed by the '-ing' form of a verb. Example: I'm interested in learning Spanish.

leaves.title: V-ING: WITH NOTIONAL SUBJECT (expressed as possessive pronouns)
leaves.grammarPoint: V-ING: WITH NOTIONAL SUBJECT (expressed as possessive pronouns)
leaves.explanation: Use a possessive before an '-ing' form to show whose action it is. Example: I don't mind his coming late.

leaves.title: VERB V-ING
leaves.explanation: Use 'verb + -ing' when a verb is followed directly by a gerund. Example: I enjoy reading.

leaves.title: VERB not V-ING
leaves.explanation: Use 'verb + not + -ing' to negate the gerund after certain verbs. Example: I regret not asking.

leaves.title: VERB OBJECT V-ING
leaves.explanation: Use 'verb + object + -ing' when a verb takes an object before the gerund. Example: I saw him leaving.

leaves.title: VERB OBJECT not V-ING
leaves.explanation: Use 'verb + object + not + -ing' to negate the object's action. Example: I understand him not wanting to go.

leaves.title: IMPERATIVE (BE) — AFF. IMP.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Be' at the start of a sentence to give a command about a state. Example: Be quiet!

leaves.title: IMPERATIVE (BE) — NEG. IMP
leaves.explanation: Add 'don't' before 'be' to give a negative command about a state. Example: Don't be late.

leaves.title: IMPERATIVE: AFFIRMATIVE (lexical verbs) — AFF. IMP.
leaves.explanation: Use the base verb at the start of a sentence to give a command. Example: Close the door.

leaves.title: IMPERATIVE: AFFIRMATIVE (lexical verbs) — NEG. IMP
leaves.explanation: Add 'don't' before the base verb to give a negative command. Example: Don't touch that.

leaves.title: Do+IMPERATIVE
leaves.explanation: Add 'Do' before an imperative to make it more emphatic or polite. Example: Do come in.

leaves.title: Please+INFINITIVE
leaves.explanation: Add 'Please' before an imperative to make a polite request. Example: Please sit down.

leaves.title: Please+don't/never+INFINITIVE
leaves.explanation: Add 'Please don't/never' before an imperative to make a polite negative request. Example: Please don't shout.

leaves.title: let's (not followed by 'not')
leaves.explanation: Use 'Let's + base verb' to suggest doing something together. Example: Let's go to the beach.

leaves.title: let's not
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after 'Let's' to suggest not doing something together. Example: Let's not argue about this.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: be able to — AFF. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: MODAL/AUX: be able to — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'be able to + base verb' to talk about ability, especially outside the simple present/past. Example: She will be able to help tomorrow.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: be able to — NEG. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: MODAL/AUX: be able to — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after 'be' to say someone lacks ability. Example: I am not able to attend.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: be able to — AFF. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: MODAL/AUX: be able to — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert 'be' and the subject to ask about ability. Example: Are you able to come?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: be able to — NEG. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: MODAL/AUX: be able to — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask about lack of ability. Example: Aren't you able to swim?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: be going to — AFF. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: MODAL/AUX: be going to — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'be going to + base verb' for a plan or intention decided before speaking. Example: I am going to start a new job.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: be going to — NEG. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: MODAL/AUX: be going to — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to make a 'going to' statement about intention negative. Example: We are not going to sell the house.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: be going to — AFF. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: MODAL/AUX: be going to — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert 'be' and the subject to ask about an intention. Example: Is he going to call her?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: be going to — NEG. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: MODAL/AUX: be going to — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask about an intention. Example: Aren't you going to eat?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: can — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'can' to talk about present ability or permission. Example: I can swim.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: can — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' (can't) to say something is not possible or not allowed. Example: I can't come tonight.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: can — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Put 'can' before the subject to ask about ability or permission. Example: Can you drive?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: can — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'can't' to ask a negative ability/permission question. Example: Can't you help me?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: could — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'could' for past ability or a polite request. Example: I could swim when I was five.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: could — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' (couldn't) to say something wasn't possible or a polite request was declined. Example: I couldn't find my keys.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: could — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Put 'could' before the subject to ask a polite question. Example: Could you help me?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: could — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'couldn't' to ask a negative polite question. Example: Couldn't you wait a moment?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: dare (to) — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'dare (to)' to talk about having the courage to do something. Example: He dared to speak up.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: dare (to) — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to say someone lacks the courage to do something. Example: She didn't dare to ask.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: dare (to) — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'dare' in a question about courage. Example: How dare you say that?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: dare (to) — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask about courage. Example: Didn't you dare to tell her?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: had better — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'had better + base verb' to give strong advice about the immediate situation. Example: You had better hurry.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: had better — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after 'better' to give negative strong advice. Example: You had better not be late.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: have to — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'have to + base verb' for an obligation, often from outside the speaker. Example: I have to work on Saturday.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: have to — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'don't/doesn't have to' to say there is no obligation. Example: You don't have to come.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: have to — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Do/Does + subject + have to' to ask about obligation. Example: Do you have to leave now?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: have to — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask about a lack of obligation. Example: Don't you have to be there at nine?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: (have) got to
leaves.explanation: Use '(have) got to + base verb' as an informal way to express obligation. Example: I've got to go now.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: have got to — NEG. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: MODAL/AUX: have got to — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'haven't/hasn't got to' to say there's no obligation, informally. Example: You haven't got to finish today.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: have got to — AFF. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: MODAL/AUX: have got to — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Have/Has + subject + got to' to ask about obligation informally. Example: Have you got to work late?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: have got to — NEG. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: MODAL/AUX: have got to — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask about a lack of obligation informally. Example: Haven't you got to leave soon?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: may — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'may' to talk about formal permission or possibility. Example: You may leave now.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: may — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to say something is not permitted or possible. Example: You may not enter.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: may — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'may' in a formal question about permission. Example: May I ask a question?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: may — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask about permission or possibility. Example: May I not know the reason?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: may as well — AFF. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: MODAL/AUX: may as well — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'may as well' to suggest doing something because there's no better option. Example: We may as well leave now.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: may as well — NEG. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: MODAL/AUX: may as well — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to suggest it's not worth doing something. Example: You may as well not bother.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: may as well — AFF. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: MODAL/AUX: may as well — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'may as well' in a suggestion-style question. Example: May we as well start now?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: may as well — NEG. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: MODAL/AUX: may as well — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form for a suggestion-style question. Example: May we as well not wait?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: may well — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'may well' to say something is quite likely. Example: It may well rain later.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: may well — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to say something is unlikely, though this form is rare. Example: It may well not happen.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: may well — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'may well' in a question about likelihood, though this form is rare. Example: May it well be true?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: may well — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask about unlikelihood, though this form is rare. Example: May it well not be true?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: might — B1.1
leaves.explanation: Use 'might' to talk about a weaker possibility than 'may'. Example: It might rain tomorrow.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: might
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' (might not) to say something is possibly not true. Example: She might not come.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: might
leaves.explanation: Use 'might' in a question about possibility. Example: Might it rain later?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: might
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask about possibility. Example: Might it not rain after all?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: might as well
leaves.explanation: Use 'might as well' to suggest an option with nothing to lose. Example: We might as well try.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: might as well
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to suggest something isn't worth doing. Example: You might as well not ask.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: might as well
leaves.explanation: Use 'might as well' in a suggestion-style question. Example: Might we as well leave?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: might as well
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form for a suggestion-style question. Example: Might we as well not stay?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: might well
leaves.explanation: Use 'might well' to say something is fairly likely. Example: She might well be right.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: might well
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to say something is possibly not the case. Example: It might well not matter.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: might well
leaves.explanation: Use 'might well' in a question about likelihood. Example: Might it well happen?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: might well
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask about likelihood. Example: Might it well not happen?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: must — B1.1
leaves.explanation: Use 'must' for strong obligation or a confident conclusion. Example: You must wear a seatbelt.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: must
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' (mustn't) to say something is forbidden. Example: You mustn't smoke here.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: must
leaves.explanation: Use 'must' in a question about obligation. Example: Must I finish this today?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: must
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask about a lack of obligation. Example: Mustn't we hurry?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: need (to) — A2.2
leaves.explanation: Use 'need (to)' to talk about necessity. Example: I need to buy milk.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: need (to)
leaves.explanation: Use 'don't/doesn't need to' to say something isn't necessary. Example: You don't need to worry.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: need (to)
leaves.explanation: Use 'Do/Does + subject + need to' to ask about necessity. Example: Do you need to leave early?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: need (to)
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask about a lack of necessity. Example: Don't you need to sleep?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: ought to — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'ought to' to give advice or state what is expected, similar to 'should'. Example: You ought to apologise.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: ought to — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to give negative advice. Example: You ought not to worry.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: ought to — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'ought to' in a question about advice, though rare in modern English. Example: Ought we to leave now?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: ought to — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask about advice, though rare. Example: Ought we not to wait?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: shall — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'shall' for formal offers or suggestions, mainly with I/we. Example: Shall we dance?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: shall — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' for a formal negative statement with 'shall'. Example: I shall not attend.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: shall — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'shall' to make a formal offer or suggestion. Example: Shall I open the window?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: shall — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a formal question with 'shall'. Example: Shall we not go together?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: should — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'should' to give advice or say what is expected. Example: You should see a doctor.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: should — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' (shouldn't) to give negative advice. Example: You shouldn't skip breakfast.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: should — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'should' in a question asking for advice. Example: Should I call her?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: should — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask about advice. Example: Shouldn't we tell him?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: used to — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'used to + base verb' for a past habit or state that no longer happens. Example: I used to live in Rome.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: used to — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'didn't use to' to say something wasn't a past habit. Example: She didn't use to like coffee.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: used to — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Did + subject + use to' to ask about a past habit. Example: Did you use to play piano?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: used to — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask about a past habit. Example: Didn't you use to smoke?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: will — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'will' for future predictions, promises, or spontaneous decisions. Example: I will help you.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: will — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' (won't) to make a future statement negative. Example: I won't forget.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: will — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'will' in a question about the future. Example: Will you come?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: will — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask about the future. Example: Won't you stay longer?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: would — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'would' for hypothetical situations or polite requests. Example: I would love to help.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: would — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' (wouldn't) for a negative hypothetical statement or refusal. Example: I wouldn't do that.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: would — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'would' in a polite or hypothetical question. Example: Would you like some tea?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: would — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form for a polite or hypothetical question. Example: Wouldn't you like to join us?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: would rather — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'would rather + base verb' to express a preference. Example: I would rather stay home.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: would rather — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to express a negative preference. Example: I would rather not go.

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: would rather — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use 'would rather' in a question about preference. Example: Would you rather walk?

leaves.title: MODAL/AUX: would rather — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask about preference. Example: Wouldn't you rather drive?

leaves.title: AUX+PROGRESSIVE — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use a modal + 'be + verb-ing' to talk about an ongoing action with modal meaning. Example: She must be sleeping.

leaves.title: AUX+PROGRESSIVE — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after the modal to make it negative. Example: He can't be joking.

leaves.title: AUX+PROGRESSIVE — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert the modal and subject before 'be + verb-ing' to ask a question. Example: Could she be joking?

leaves.title: AUX+PROGRESSIVE — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask about an ongoing action with modal meaning. Example: Can't he be waiting outside?

leaves.title: AUX+PERFECT — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use a modal + 'have + past participle' to talk about a past possibility or conclusion. Example: She must have left already.

leaves.title: AUX+PERFECT — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after the modal to negate a past modal statement. Example: He can't have finished yet.

leaves.title: AUX+PERFECT — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert the modal and subject before 'have + past participle' to ask a question. Example: Could they have known?

leaves.title: AUX+PERFECT — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask about a past possibility. Example: Shouldn't she have called by now?

leaves.title: there+be — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'there + be' to say that something exists. Example: There is a cat in the garden.

leaves.title: there+be — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after 'be' to say something doesn't exist. Example: There isn't any milk.

leaves.title: there+be — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert 'be' and 'there' to ask if something exists. Example: Is there a problem?

leaves.title: there+be — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask if something doesn't exist. Example: Isn't there a solution?

leaves.title: there+have/has+been — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'there + have/has + been' to say something has existed or happened up to now. Example: There has been an accident.

leaves.title: there+have/has+been — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to say something hasn't happened. Example: There hasn't been any news.

leaves.title: there+have/has+been — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert 'have/has' and 'there' to ask if something has happened. Example: Has there been a mistake?

leaves.title: there+have/has+been — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask if something hasn't happened. Example: Hasn't there been enough time?

leaves.title: there+AUX+be — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'there + modal + be' to say something might/should/will exist. Example: There will be a meeting tomorrow.

leaves.title: there+AUX+be — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after the modal to say something won't/shouldn't exist. Example: There won't be enough seats.

leaves.title: there+AUX+be — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert the modal and 'there' to ask if something will/might exist. Example: Will there be food?

leaves.title: there+AUX+be — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask if something won't exist. Example: Won't there be a delay?

leaves.title: here is/are
leaves.explanation: Use 'Here is/are' to introduce something nearby, often when giving or showing it. Example: Here is your ticket.

leaves.title: COORDINATING CONJUNCTIONS
leaves.explanation: Coordinating conjunctions (and, but, or, so, yet) join words, phrases, or clauses of equal importance. Example: I like tea and coffee.

leaves.title: the fact(s) that+CLAUSE
leaves.explanation: Use 'the fact(s) that + clause' to introduce a statement as an established fact. Example: The fact that he apologised helped.

leaves.title: V+that+CLAUSE
leaves.explanation: Use 'verb + that + clause' when a verb reports what someone thinks, says, or believes. Example: I think that you're right.

leaves.title: know/wonder+WH-(CLAUSE) (except for 'whether')
leaves.explanation: Use 'know/wonder + wh-word + clause' to report a question indirectly. Example: I wonder where she went.

leaves.title: whether
leaves.explanation: Use 'whether' to introduce an indirect yes/no question or a choice between alternatives. Example: I don't know whether to go.

leaves.title: ADVERBIAL CLAUSE: when
leaves.explanation: Use 'when' to introduce a clause showing the time something happens. Example: I'll call when I arrive.

leaves.title: ADVERBIAL CLAUSE: if
leaves.explanation: Use 'if' to introduce a conditional clause. Example: If it rains, we'll stay inside.

leaves.title: ADVERBIAL CLAUSE: as
leaves.explanation: Use 'as' to introduce a clause showing time, reason, or manner. Example: As I was leaving, the phone rang.

leaves.title: ADVERBIAL CLAUSE: as soon as
leaves.explanation: Use 'as soon as' to introduce a clause showing something happens immediately after another. Example: Call me as soon as you arrive.

leaves.title: ADVERBIAL CLAUSE: by the time
leaves.explanation: Use 'by the time' to introduce a clause showing a deadline for another event. Example: By the time we arrived, the film had started.

leaves.title: ADVERBIAL CLAUSE: so that
leaves.explanation: Use 'so that' to introduce a clause showing purpose or result. Example: She left early so that she wouldn't be late.

leaves.title: SUBORDINATE CLAUSE: after/albeit/although/because/before/despite/except/for/lest/like/once/since/so/than/though/till/unless/until/where/whereas/wheresoever/whether/while/whilst tagged as IN
leaves.explanation: Subordinating conjunctions (although, because, before, since, unless, while, etc.) introduce a dependent clause. Example: I stayed home because I was ill.

leaves.title: hope/know/think+CLAUSE (without 'that')
leaves.explanation: Use 'hope/know/think + clause' without 'that' in informal speech and writing. Example: I hope you're feeling better.

leaves.title: it+BE(+ADV)+ADJ(+for+NP)+to+INFINITIVE — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'It is + adjective (+ for someone) + to-infinitive' to comment on an action. Example: It is important for you to arrive on time.

leaves.title: it+BE(+ADV)+ADJ(+for+NP)+to+INFINITIVE — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after 'be' to make this pattern negative. Example: It is not easy to explain.

leaves.title: it+BE(+ADV)+ADJ(+for+NP)+to+INFINITIVE — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert 'be' and 'it' to ask a question with this pattern. Example: Is it difficult to learn?

leaves.title: it+BE(+ADV)+ADJ(+for+NP)+to+INFINITIVE — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a question with this pattern. Example: Isn't it hard to understand?

leaves.title: V+it+ADJ(+for+NP)+to+INFINITIVE
leaves.explanation: Use 'verb + it + adjective (+ for someone) + to-infinitive' with verbs like 'find' or 'make'. Example: I find it hard to concentrate.

leaves.title: it+BE(+ADV)+ADJ+that+CLAUSE — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'It is + adjective + that + clause' to comment on a fact using a that-clause. Example: It is strange that she didn't call.

leaves.title: it+BE(+ADV)+ADJ+that+CLAUSE — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' after 'be' to make this pattern negative. Example: It is not true that he left.

leaves.title: it+BE(+ADV)+ADJ+that+CLAUSE — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert 'be' and 'it' to ask a question with this pattern. Example: Is it certain that they'll come?

leaves.title: it+BE(+ADV)+ADJ+that+CLAUSE — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a question with this pattern. Example: Isn't it obvious that she's tired?

leaves.title: V+it+ADJ(+for+NP)+that+CLAUSE
leaves.explanation: Use 'verb + it + adjective (+ for someone) + that + clause' with verbs like 'think' or 'make'. Example: I think it strange that he left.

leaves.title: WH-+to+INFINITIVE
leaves.explanation: Use a wh-word + to-infinitive to express uncertainty about how, what, when, etc. to do something. Example: I don't know what to say.

leaves.title: PREMODIFYING PRESENT PARTICIPLE
leaves.explanation: Use a present participle before a noun to describe it. Example: a running tap

leaves.title: POSTMODIFYING PRESENT
leaves.explanation: Use a present participle after a noun to describe it, in a reduced relative clause. Example: the man standing there

leaves.title: PREMODIFYING PAST PARTICIPLE
leaves.explanation: Use a past participle before a noun to describe it. Example: a broken window

leaves.title: POSTMODIFYING PAST PARTICIPLE
leaves.explanation: Use a past participle after a noun to describe it, in a reduced relative clause. Example: the letter written by hand

leaves.title: NOMINATIVE RELATIVE PRONOUN: who
leaves.explanation: Use 'who' as the subject of a relative clause referring to a person. Example: the man who called you

leaves.title: NOMINATIVE RELATIVE PRONOUN: which
leaves.explanation: Use 'which' as the subject of a relative clause referring to a thing. Example: the book which is on the table

leaves.title: NOMINATIVE RELATIVE PRONOUN:
leaves.explanation: Use 'that' as the subject of a relative clause referring to a person or thing. Example: the dog that barked

leaves.title: ACCUSATIVE RELATIVE PRONOUN: who
leaves.explanation: Use 'who' as the object of a relative clause referring to a person, informally. Example: the woman who I met

leaves.title: ACCUSATIVE RELATIVE PRONOUN: whom
leaves.explanation: Use 'whom' as the object of a relative clause referring to a person, formally. Example: the woman whom I met

leaves.title: ACCUSATIVE RELATIVE PRONOUN: which
leaves.explanation: Use 'which' as the object of a relative clause referring to a thing. Example: the film which I watched

leaves.title: ACCUSATIVE RELATIVE PRONOUN: that
leaves.explanation: Use 'that' as the object of a relative clause referring to a person or thing. Example: the book that I read

leaves.title: ELLIPTICAL ACCUSATIVE RELATIVE PRONOUN
leaves.explanation: Omit the relative pronoun when it is the object of the clause. Example: the book I read

leaves.title: GENITIVE RELATIVE PRONOUN
leaves.explanation: Use 'whose' to show possession in a relative clause. Example: the man whose car was stolen

leaves.title: RELATIVE PRONOUN: NONRESTRICTIVE
leaves.explanation: Use a relative clause set off by commas to add extra, non-essential information. Example: My brother, who lives in Rome, is visiting.

leaves.title: PSEUDO RELATIVE PRONOUN: as
leaves.explanation: Use 'as' to introduce a relative clause commenting on the whole previous statement. Example: He was late, as usual.

leaves.title: COMPOUND RELATIVE PRONOUN:
leaves.explanation: Use compound relative pronouns (whoever, whatever, whichever) to mean 'any person/thing that'. Example: Take whatever you need.

leaves.title: PREP+RELATIVE PRONOUN
leaves.explanation: Place a preposition before a relative pronoun in formal style. Example: the house in which she lives

leaves.title: RELATIVE ADVERB: WITH
leaves.explanation: Use a relative adverb (where, when, why) with a stated antecedent. Example: the city where I was born

leaves.title: RELATIVE ADVERB: WITHOUT ANTECEDENT
leaves.explanation: Use a relative adverb (where, when, why) without a stated antecedent. Example: That's why I left.

leaves.title: RELATIVE ADVERB: NONRESTRICTIVE
leaves.explanation: Use a relative adverb in a non-essential clause set off by commas. Example: We visited Paris, where we saw the tower.

leaves.title: WH-EVER
leaves.explanation: Add '-ever' to a wh-word (whoever, whatever, wherever) to mean 'no matter who/what/where'. Example: Whatever happens, stay calm.

leaves.title: PREPOSITION STRANDING
leaves.explanation: Leave a preposition at the end of a clause instead of before the relative pronoun. Example: This is the book I told you about.

leaves.title: EXCLAMATION: How ADJ/ADV ...!
leaves.explanation: Use 'How + adjective/adverb + subject + verb!' to express strong feeling. Example: How beautiful this is!

leaves.title: EXCLAMATION: How ...!
leaves.explanation: Use 'How + subject + verb!' to express strong feeling simply. Example: How you've grown!

leaves.title: EXCLAMATION: What ...!
leaves.explanation: Use 'What + (a/an) + noun!' to express strong feeling about something. Example: What a lovely day!

leaves.title: TAG QUESTION: FOLLOWING AFFIRMATIVE SENTENCE
leaves.explanation: Add a short question (tag) to the end of an affirmative statement to check agreement. Example: It's cold, isn't it?

leaves.title: TAG QUESTION: FOLLOWING NEGATIVE SENTENCE
leaves.explanation: Add a short positive tag to the end of a negative statement to check agreement. Example: You didn't call, did you?

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+V — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Subject + verb' as the simplest sentence pattern with no object. Example: Birds fly.

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+V — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to negate the simple subject-verb pattern. Example: Birds don't fly at night.

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+V — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert the auxiliary and subject to ask a question with this pattern. Example: Do birds fly?

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+V — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a question with this pattern. Example: Don't birds fly south?

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+BECOME/FEEL/GO/LOOK/SEEM/SOUND+COMPLEMENT (ADJ) — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Subject + become/feel/look/seem + adjective' to describe a change or state. Example: She became famous.

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+BECOME/FEEL/GO/LOOK/SEEM/SOUND+COMPLEMENT (ADJ) — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to negate this pattern. Example: He doesn't seem happy.

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+BECOME/FEEL/GO/LOOK/SEEM/SOUND+COMPLEMENT (ADJ) — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert the auxiliary and subject to ask a question with this pattern. Example: Does she seem tired?

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+BECOME/FEEL/GO/LOOK/SEEM/SOUND+COMPLEMENT (ADJ) — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a question with this pattern. Example: Doesn't he look well?

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+V+OBJECT — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Subject + verb + object' as a basic transitive sentence pattern. Example: She reads books.

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+V+OBJECT — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to negate a subject-verb-object sentence. Example: She doesn't read newspapers.

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+V+OBJECT — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert the auxiliary and subject to ask a question with this pattern. Example: Does she read novels?

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+V+OBJECT — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a question with this pattern. Example: Doesn't she like reading?

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL+INDIRECT OBJECT+DIRECT OBJECT — AFF. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL+INDIRECT OBJECT+DIRECT OBJECT — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Subject + verb + indirect object + direct object' with verbs like give/show/tell. Example: I gave her a gift.

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL+INDIRECT OBJECT+DIRECT OBJECT — NEG. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL+INDIRECT OBJECT+DIRECT OBJECT — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to negate this double-object pattern. Example: I didn't give her a gift.

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL+INDIRECT OBJECT+DIRECT OBJECT — AFF. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL+INDIRECT OBJECT+DIRECT OBJECT — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert the auxiliary and subject to ask a question with this pattern. Example: Did you give her a gift?

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL+INDIRECT OBJECT+DIRECT OBJECT — NEG. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL+INDIRECT OBJECT+DIRECT OBJECT — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a question with this pattern. Example: Didn't you show him the way?

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL+DIRECT OBJECT+to+INDIRECT OBJECT — AFF. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL+DIRECT OBJECT+to+INDIRECT OBJECT — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Subject + verb + direct object + to + indirect object' as an alternative to the double-object pattern. Example: I gave a gift to her.

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL+DIRECT OBJECT+to+INDIRECT OBJECT — NEG. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL+DIRECT OBJECT+to+INDIRECT OBJECT — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to negate this pattern. Example: I didn't give a gift to her.

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL+DIRECT OBJECT+to+INDIRECT OBJECT — AFF. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL+DIRECT OBJECT+to+INDIRECT OBJECT — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert the auxiliary and subject to ask a question with this pattern. Example: Did you send the letter to him?

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL+DIRECT OBJECT+to+INDIRECT OBJECT — NEG. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL+DIRECT OBJECT+to+INDIRECT OBJECT — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a question with this pattern. Example: Didn't you show the report to her?

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+MAKE+OBJECT+COMPLEME NT (ADJ) — AFF. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+MAKE+OBJECT+COMPLEME NT (ADJ) — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'Subject + make + object + adjective' to show a result caused by the subject. Example: The news made her happy.

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+MAKE+OBJECT+COMPLEME NT (ADJ) — NEG. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+MAKE+OBJECT+COMPLEME NT (ADJ) — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to negate this causative pattern. Example: The film didn't make him sad.

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+MAKE+OBJECT+COMPLEME NT (ADJ) — AFF. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+MAKE+OBJECT+COMPLEME NT (ADJ) — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert the auxiliary and subject to ask a question with this pattern. Example: Did the news make you nervous?

leaves.title: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+MAKE+OBJECT+COMPLEME NT (ADJ) — NEG. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+MAKE+OBJECT+COMPLEME NT (ADJ) — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a question with this pattern. Example: Didn't that make you angry?

leaves.title: INDIRECT SPEECH: SAY/EXPLAIN/REPORT
leaves.explanation: Report what someone said using 'say/explain/report + that + clause', usually changing tense and pronouns. Example: She said that she was tired.

leaves.title: INDIRECT SPEECH: TELL
leaves.explanation: Report what someone told another person using 'tell + person + that + clause'. Example: He told me that he was leaving.

leaves.title: INDIRECT QUESTION: DECIDE/EXPLAIN/KNOW/LEARN/SEE/UNDERSTAND/WONDER
leaves.explanation: Report a question using 'decide/explain/know/wonder + wh-word + clause'. Example: I don't know why she left.

leaves.title: INDIRECT QUESTION: ASK/REMIND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL
leaves.explanation: Report a question directed at someone using 'ask/remind/tell + person + wh-word + clause'. Example: She asked me where I lived.

leaves.title: CLEFT SENTENCE FOCUSING ON PREPOSITIONAL PHRASE/ADVERB — AFF. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: CLEFT SENTENCE FOCUSING ON PREPOSITIONAL PHRASE/ADVERB — AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'It is + prepositional phrase/adverb + that/who ...' to emphasise that part of the sentence. Example: It was in Paris that we met.

leaves.title: CLEFT SENTENCE FOCUSING ON PREPOSITIONAL PHRASE/ADVERB — NEG. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: CLEFT SENTENCE FOCUSING ON PREPOSITIONAL PHRASE/ADVERB — NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to negate this emphasis (cleft) pattern. Example: It wasn't in Paris that we met.

leaves.title: CLEFT SENTENCE FOCUSING ON PREPOSITIONAL PHRASE/ADVERB — AFF. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: CLEFT SENTENCE FOCUSING ON PREPOSITIONAL PHRASE/ADVERB — AFF. INT.
leaves.explanation: Invert 'be' and 'it' to ask a question with this emphasis pattern. Example: Was it yesterday that you called?

leaves.title: CLEFT SENTENCE FOCUSING ON PREPOSITIONAL PHRASE/ADVERB — NEG. INT.
leaves.grammarPoint: CLEFT SENTENCE FOCUSING ON PREPOSITIONAL PHRASE/ADVERB — NEG. INT.
leaves.explanation: Use a negative form to ask a question with this pattern. Example: Wasn't it you who called?

leaves.title: PSEUDO-CLEFT SENTENCE: WHAT — (MAIN CLAUSE) AFF. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: PSEUDO-CLEFT SENTENCE: WHAT — (MAIN CLAUSE) AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'What + clause + is/was + ...' to emphasise part of a sentence. Example: What I need is some rest.

leaves.title: PSEUDO-CLEFT SENTENCE: WHAT — (MAIN CLAUSE) NEG. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: PSEUDO-CLEFT SENTENCE: WHAT — (MAIN CLAUSE) NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to negate this emphasis (pseudo-cleft) pattern. Example: What I need is not money.

leaves.title: HAVE/LET/MAKE+NP+INFINITIVE
