leaves.explanation: Use 'have/let/make + noun + base verb' (causative) to say someone causes another to do something. Example: I had him fix the car.

leaves.title: HAVE/GET+NP+PAST PARTICIPLE
leaves.explanation: Use 'have/get + noun + past participle' to say someone arranges for something to be done. Example: I had my hair cut.

leaves.title: GET+NP+PRESENT PARTICIPLE
leaves.explanation: Use 'get + noun + present participle' to say someone causes an action to start happening. Example: I got the engine running.

leaves.title: ASK/TELL+NP+to+INFINITIVE
leaves.explanation: Use 'ask/tell + noun + to-infinitive' to report a request or instruction given to someone. Example: She asked me to wait.

leaves.title: FEEL/HEAR/SEE+NP+INFINITIVE
leaves.explanation: Use 'feel/hear/see + noun + base verb' to describe perceiving a complete action. Example: I saw him leave.

leaves.title: FEEL/HEAR/SEE+NP+PRESENT PARTICIPLE
leaves.explanation: Use 'feel/hear/see + noun + present participle' to describe perceiving an action in progress. Example: I heard her singing.

leaves.title: FEEL/HEAR/SEE+NP+PAST PARTICIPLE
leaves.explanation: Use 'feel/hear/see + noun + past participle' to describe perceiving something that has happened to it. Example: I saw the window broken.

leaves.title: PARTICIPIAL CONSTRUCTION: PRESENT PARTICIPLE — (SUBORDINATE CLAUSE) AFF. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: PARTICIPIAL CONSTRUCTION: PRESENT PARTICIPLE — (SUBORDINATE CLAUSE) AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use a present participle clause to show an action happening alongside the main clause. Example: Walking home, I saw an old friend.

leaves.title: PARTICIPIAL CONSTRUCTION: PRESENT PARTICIPLE — (SUBORDINATE CLAUSE) NEG. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: PARTICIPIAL CONSTRUCTION: PRESENT PARTICIPLE — (SUBORDINATE CLAUSE) NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' before the present participle to negate this construction. Example: Not knowing the answer, she stayed silent.

leaves.title: PARTICIPIAL CONSTRUCTION: PAST PARTICIPLE — (SUBORDINATE CLAUSE) AFF. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: PARTICIPIAL CONSTRUCTION: PAST PARTICIPLE — (SUBORDINATE CLAUSE) AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use a past participle clause to show a passive action related to the main clause. Example: Written in haste, the letter had errors.

leaves.title: PARTICIPIAL CONSTRUCTION: PAST PARTICIPLE — (SUBORDINATE CLAUSE) NEG. DEC.
leaves.grammarPoint: PARTICIPIAL CONSTRUCTION: PAST PARTICIPLE — (SUBORDINATE CLAUSE) NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' before the past participle to negate this construction. Example: Not convinced, he asked more questions.

leaves.title: CONDITIONAL: SECOND — (SUBORDINATE CLAUSE) AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use the second conditional ('if + past simple, would + base verb') for unreal present/future situations. Example: If I had more time, I would travel.

leaves.title: CONDITIONAL: SECOND — (SUBORDINATE CLAUSE) NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to make part of a second conditional negative. Example: If it weren't raining, we would go out.

leaves.title: CONDITIONAL: THIRD — (SUBORDINATE CLAUSE) AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use the third conditional ('if + past perfect, would have + past participle') for unreal past situations. Example: If I had known, I would have helped.

leaves.title: CONDITIONAL: THIRD — (SUBORDINATE CLAUSE) NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' to make part of a third conditional negative. Example: If she hadn't called, I wouldn't have known.

leaves.title: DEMAND/INSIST/ORDER/PROPOSE/RECOMMEND/REQUIRE/SUGGEST+NP+INFINITIVE — (SUBORDINATE CLAUSE) AFF. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Use 'demand/insist/suggest + that + subject + base verb' (subjunctive) after verbs of urging. Example: I suggest that he arrive early.

leaves.title: DEMAND/INSIST/ORDER/PROPOSE/RECOMMEND/REQUIRE/SUGGEST+NP+INFINITIVE — (SUBORDINATE CLAUSE) NEG. DEC.
leaves.explanation: Add 'not' before the base verb in this subjunctive pattern. Example: I insist that she not leave.

leaves.title: WISH+SECOND CONDITIONAL
leaves.explanation: Use 'wish + past simple/continuous' to express a wish about a present unreal situation. Example: I wish I had more free time.

leaves.title: WISH+THIRD CONDITIONAL
leaves.explanation: Use 'wish + past perfect' to express regret about a past situation. Example: I wish I had studied harder.

leaves.title: AS IF/THOUGH+SECOND CONDITIONAL
leaves.explanation: Use 'as if/as though + past simple' to describe an unreal present comparison. Example: He talks as if he knew everything.

leaves.title: AS IF/THOUGH+THIRD CONDITIONAL
leaves.explanation: Use 'as if/as though + past perfect' to describe an unreal past comparison. Example: She looked as if she had seen a ghost.

leaves.title: IF ONLY+SECOND CONDITIONAL
leaves.explanation: Use 'if only + past simple' to express a strong wish about the present. Example: If only I knew the answer.

leaves.title: IF ONLY+THIRD CONDITIONAL
leaves.explanation: Use 'if only + past perfect' to express strong regret about the past. Example: If only I had listened to her.

leaves.title: IF+SHOULD (e.g. if it should rain tomorrow)
leaves.grammarPoint: IF+SHOULD (e.g. if it should rain tomorrow)
leaves.explanation: Use 'if + should' to describe an unlikely future condition, formally. Example: If it should rain tomorrow, we'll cancel.

leaves.title: INVERSION: SECOND CONDITIONAL (e.g. Were I in your place, ....)
leaves.grammarPoint: INVERSION: SECOND CONDITIONAL (e.g. Were I in your place, ....)
leaves.explanation: Invert 'were' and the subject instead of using 'if' in a second conditional, formally. Example: Were I in your place, I would apologise.

leaves.title: INVERSION: THIRD CONDITIONAL (e.g. Had I known it, ....)
leaves.grammarPoint: INVERSION: THIRD CONDITIONAL (e.g. Had I known it, ....)
leaves.explanation: Invert 'had' and the subject instead of using 'if' in a third conditional, formally. Example: Had I known, I would have come.

leaves.title: INVERSION: CONDITIONAL WITH SHOULD (e.g. Should it rain tomorrow.....)
leaves.grammarPoint: INVERSION: CONDITIONAL WITH SHOULD (e.g. Should it rain tomorrow.....)
leaves.explanation: Invert 'should' and the subject instead of using 'if', formally. Example: Should it rain, we'll stay inside.

leaves.title: if it were not for ...
leaves.explanation: Use 'if it were not for ...' to say something is essential to a present situation. Example: If it weren't for you, I'd be lost.

leaves.title: were it not for ...
leaves.explanation: Invert 'were' and 'it' instead of 'if' to say something is essential, formally. Example: Were it not for your help, I'd have failed.

leaves.title: if it hadn't been for ...
leaves.explanation: Use 'if it hadn't been for ...' to say something was essential to a past situation. Example: If it hadn't been for the rain, we'd have won.

leaves.title: had it not been for ...
leaves.explanation: Invert 'had' and 'it' instead of 'if' to say something was essential to a past outcome, formally. Example: Had it not been for you, I'd have given up.

leaves.title: INVERSION: so+BE/HAVE/DO/AUX+PERSONAL PRON
leaves.explanation: Use 'So + auxiliary + subject' to agree with a positive statement. Example: I love coffee. So do I.

leaves.title: INVERSION: neither/nor+BE/HAVE/DO/AUX+PERSONAL PRON
leaves.explanation: Use 'Neither/Nor + auxiliary + subject' to agree with a negative statement. Example: I don't like coffee. Neither do I.

leaves.title: INVERSION: Hardly/Little/Never/No sooner/Scarcely/Seldom ....
leaves.explanation: Move a negative adverb (Hardly, Never, No sooner) to the front of a sentence and invert the verb for emphasis. Example: Never have I seen such a mess.

leaves.title: WH- QUESTION: Why ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Why ...?' to ask about a reason. Example: Why are you late?

leaves.title: WH- QUESTION: When ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'When ...?' to ask about a time. Example: When does the film start?

leaves.title: WH- QUESTION: Who ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Who ...?' to ask about the subject of a sentence, referring to a person. Example: Who called you?

leaves.title: WH- QUESTION: Whom ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Whom ...?' to ask about the object of a sentence, referring to a person, formally. Example: Whom did you meet?

leaves.title: WH- QUESTION: What ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'What ...?' to ask about a thing or action. Example: What happened?

leaves.title: WH- QUESTION: What N ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'What + noun ...?' to ask about a specific type of thing. Example: What time is it?

leaves.title: WH- QUESTION: Which ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Which ...?' to ask about a choice among a limited set. Example: Which do you prefer?

leaves.title: WH- QUESTION: Which N ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Which + noun ...?' to ask about a choice among a limited set of things. Example: Which bus goes downtown?

leaves.title: WH- QUESTION: Whose ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Whose ...?' to ask about ownership. Example: Whose is this?

leaves.title: WH- QUESTION: Whose N ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Whose + noun ...?' to ask about ownership of a specific thing. Example: Whose bag is this?

leaves.title: WH- QUESTION: Where ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Where ...?' to ask about a place. Example: Where do you live?

leaves.title: WH- QUESTION: How ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'How ...?' to ask about manner or method. Example: How did you do that?

leaves.title: WH- QUESTION: How ADJ/ADV ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'How + adjective/adverb ...?' to ask about degree. Example: How old are you?

leaves.title: WH- QUESTION: PREP what/which/whom/whose ...?
leaves.explanation: Put a preposition before a wh-word in a formal question. Example: To what do I owe this visit?

leaves.title: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Can you ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Can you ...?' to make an informal request. Example: Can you help me?

leaves.title: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Can't you ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Can't you ...?' to make an informal, slightly urging request. Example: Can't you just try?

leaves.title: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Could you ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Could you ...?' to make a polite request. Example: Could you pass the salt?

leaves.title: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Couldn't you ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Couldn't you ...?' to make a polite, slightly pressing request. Example: Couldn't you stay a little longer?

leaves.title: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Will you ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Will you ...?' to make a request or ask about willingness. Example: Will you close the door?

leaves.title: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Won't you ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Won't you ...?' to make an inviting request. Example: Won't you join us?

leaves.title: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Would you ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Would you ...?' to make a polite request. Example: Would you mind waiting?

leaves.title: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Wouldn't you ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Wouldn't you ...?' to make a polite, persuasive request. Example: Wouldn't you like to try this?

leaves.title: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Can I ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Can I ...?' to ask for permission informally. Example: Can I sit here?

leaves.title: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Could I ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Could I ...?' to ask for permission more politely. Example: Could I ask a question?

leaves.title: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: May I ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'May I ...?' to ask for permission formally. Example: May I come in?

leaves.title: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Shall I ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Shall I ...?' to offer to do something. Example: Shall I open the window?

leaves.title: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Shall we ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Shall we ...?' to suggest doing something together. Example: Shall we begin?

leaves.title: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Should I ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Should I ...?' to ask for advice. Example: Should I call her now?

leaves.title: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Why don't you ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Why don't you ...?' to make a suggestion to someone else. Example: Why don't you take a break?

leaves.title: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Why don't we ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Why don't we ...?' to make a suggestion including yourself. Example: Why don't we order pizza?

leaves.title: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Why not ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'Why not ...?' to make a casual suggestion. Example: Why not try the new restaurant?

leaves.title: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: How about ...?
leaves.explanation: Use 'How about ...?' to suggest an idea or option. Example: How about going for a walk?
